title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: a school that wants to list everything there is opens its book with one word you wouldn't expect: dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday we left Nyaya, logic, at dusk: the post or the person, and doubt as the doorway to a search that ends in release. Did you let one doubt start an honest search? A second school opens today. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.
screen: `NYAYA: FROM DOUBT TO RELEASE.` · `A NEW SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: A sack of rice has split on the kitchen floor. Grains everywhere, under the stove, in the corners, between the tiles. You crouch down and start picking them up, one by one, and somewhere in there a strange thought arrives: this whole sack, this whole meal, is only ever grains. Little things, counted up. There's a story people tell about the sage who founded today's school. They say his name, Kanada, came from his habit of living on grains, gleaned one by one from harvested fields. Whether or not that's history, it fits. Because his school would go on to say the world itself is made of tiny grains.
screen: `RICE ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `ONLY EVER GRAINS.` → `KANADA, THE GRAIN-GATHERER.`

segments.voice: The school is Vaisheshika, and its root text is the Vaisheshika Sutra, credited to Kanada. You might expect a book about the building blocks of the world to open with matter. It doesn't. Its first sutra says, in effect: now, therefore, we will explain dharma. And the next one says what dharma is: that from which come both rising up in this world and the highest good. So before a single atom appears, the school tells you why it's counting at all. Knowing what the world is made of, and how things really differ from one another, is meant to serve a good life and, finally, freedom. That's the same note Nyaya struck. And the two schools are close neighbors. Later thinkers joined them, so often you'll hear them named together, Nyaya-Vaisheshika: one asking how we know, the other asking what there is to know. Then there's the name. Tradition links Vaisheshika to vishesha, particularity: the thing that makes one thing this one and not that one. Later teachers of the school took it all the way down: two of the tiniest particles of earth, alike in every quality, are still not copies, and vishesha is what keeps each one itself. The school is known for its atoms, and we'll get to them tomorrow. But notice the starting point. It isn't that everything is one blur. It's that everything is particular. Carried out of the classroom, that idea turns tender. The grain on the floor, the stranger on the bus, the person who annoys you: each is particular, really itself, not interchangeable. A school of atoms that begins with dharma refuses to let anything be just another one.
screen: `THE SUTRA OF KANADA.` · `IT OPENS WITH DHARMA.` · `A NEIGHBOR TO NYAYA.` · `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS JUST ANOTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice particulars. Settle, and breathe. Then pick something small near you: a grain of rice, a button, a leaf, the tip of your own finger. Look at it as if it were the only one. Its exact edge. Its color in this light. The tiny mark that no other has. When the mind says, it's just a button, come back and look again. Then, if you like, let one person come to mind, and see them the same way: not a type, not a role, but this one. If you pray, you can give thanks for this one thing, exactly as it is. The bell holds the time.
Vaisheshika. The school of Kanada, linked by tradition to vishesha, particularity, and known for its atoms. Its sutra opens with dharma.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Today, look at one person or thing you usually lump in with the rest, and see the one particular thing it really is. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Vaisheshika is studied in traditional Sanskrit schools alongside Nyaya, often as one joined system, through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries.

fork.setup: you're writing a book that will list everything the world is made of. what do you put in the very first line?
fork.reveal: the Vaisheshika Sutra begins, in effect: now we will explain dharma. the counting is meant to serve a good life and the highest good.

original.note: Sanskrit: Vaisheshika, the school whose name tradition links to vishesha, particularity.

trapdoor: what you thought: the school of atoms is ancient physics.
what it means: it lists what the world is made of to serve dharma and the highest good, and it starts by insisting each thing is itself.
what a scholar hears: Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.1–2: dharma is that from which come abhyudaya, worldly rising, and nihshreyasa, the highest good.
